answer_text:
Interpreting the notation in the standard paired way,

\[
\mathbb P(X_k=1)=\frac{1+k^{-1/2}}2,\qquad 
\mathbb P(X_k=-1)=\frac{1-k^{-1/2}}2 .
\]

Let

\[
S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n .
\]

First compute the mean and variance of \(X_k\). Since \(X_k^2=1\),

\[
\mathbb E[X_k]
=1\cdot \frac{1+k^{-1/2}}2+(-1)\cdot \frac{1-k^{-1/2}}2
=k^{-1/2},
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{Var}(X_k)=\mathbb E[X_k^2]-(\mathbb E[X_k])^2
=1-\frac1k.
\]

Thus

\[
\mu_n:=\mathbb E[S_n]=\sum_{k=1}^n k^{-1/2},
\qquad
\sigma_n^2:=\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=\sum_{k=1}^n\left(1-\frac1k\right)
=n-H_n,
\]

where \(H_n\) is the \(n\)-th harmonic number. Using the standard asymptotics,

\[
\mu_n=\sum_{k=1}^n k^{-1/2}=2\sqrt n+O(1),
\qquad
\sigma_n^2=n-H_n=n-\log n+O(1).
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{\mu_n}{\sigma_n}
\to 2.
\]

Now apply the Lindeberg-Feller central limit theorem to the independent centered variables \(X_k-\mathbb E[X_k]\). Since the variables are bounded and

\[
\frac{\max_{1\le k\le n}\operatorname{Var}(X_k)}{\sigma_n^2}
\to 0,
\]

the Lindeberg condition holds, and hence

\[
\frac{S_n-\mu_n}{\sigma_n}\xrightarrow{d} N(0,1).
\]

Now

\[
\mathbb P(S_n\le 0)
=
\mathbb P\left(
\frac{S_n-\mu_n}{\sigma_n}
\le -\frac{\mu_n}{\sigma_n}
\right).
\]

Since \(\mu_n/\sigma_n\to 2\), and the standard normal CDF \(\Phi\) is continuous,

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(S_n\le 0)
=
\Phi(-2).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{\Phi(-2)\approx 0.02275}.
\]
